title: Inheritance
objective: Build a child class that inherits from a parent with super().__init__(), then extends and overrides its behavior.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose, examples, and exercises are original Code Forge material using an original theme, not the book's example classes.

paragraphs: When one class is a more specific version of another, you don't need to repeat its code. A child class can inherit from a parent class by listing the parent's name in parentheses after the child's own name, as in class Child(Parent):.
Inside the child's __init__(), calling super().__init__(...) runs the parent class's __init__() for you, so the parent's attributes get set up correctly before the child adds anything of its own.

A child class isn't limited to what it inherits. It can define brand-new attributes and methods that only it has, and it can also override a method from the parent by defining a method with the same name — Python uses the child's version instead for instances of the child.
explanation.rule: A child class inherits from its parent with class Child(Parent):, calls super().__init__() to reuse the parent's setup, and can add or override methods of its own.

examples.title: Extending and Overriding a Parent Class
examples.note: Smith(Worker) inherits from Worker. super().__init__(name, shift_hours) reuses Worker's setup, self.specialty is a new attribute, forge_item() is a new method, and clock_in() overrides the parent's version entirely.

checks.question: What happens when a child class defines a method with the same name as one in its parent class?
options: The child's version overrides the parent's version for instances of the child class.
Python raises an error because the name is already used.
Both methods run every time, one after the other.
The parent's version always takes priority.

feedback.correct: Correct — a method defined on the child class overrides the parent's method of the same name.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Python looks at the child class first and uses its version if one exists.

assignment.title: Sentinel Watch
assignment.brief: Write a Guard class and a Sentinel subclass that inherits from it, adds new behavior, and overrides report().
requirements: Define a class named Guard with __init__(self, name, post) that stores self.name and self.post.
Guard has a method report() that prints f"{self.name} is stationed at {self.post}."
Define a class named Sentinel that inherits from Guard.
Sentinel's __init__(self, name, post, alert_level) calls super().__init__(name, post) and then stores self.alert_level.
Sentinel overrides report() to print f"{self.name} is stationed at {self.post} (alert level: {self.alert_level})."
Sentinel adds a new method sound_alarm() that prints f"{self.name} sounds the alarm!"
Create a Sentinel instance and call both report() and sound_alarm() on it.
assignment.testHarness:
# ---- Code Forge validation ----
import io, contextlib
_cf_buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(_cf_buf):
    _cf_watcher = Sentinel("Vex", "east gate", "red")
    _cf_watcher.report()
    _cf_watcher.sound_alarm()
_cf_result = _cf_buf.getvalue()
print("__CF_TEST_OUTPUT__")
print(repr(_cf_result))
assignment.expectedOutput:
Vex is stationed at east gate (alert level: red).
Vex sounds the alarm!
assignment.outputCheckLabel: Sentinel("Vex", "east gate", "red") reports its alert level, then sounds the alarm

hints: Guard needs its own __init__(self, name, post) and a report() method before you touch Sentinel.
Sentinel(Guard) goes in the class line to inherit from Guard.
Inside Sentinel's __init__, call super().__init__(name, post) first, then set self.alert_level = alert_level.
Define report() again inside Sentinel with the same name — that overrides the parent's version. sound_alarm() is a new method that only Sentinel has.
